q: Which cells in a taste bud divide to replace worn-out gustatory receptor cells?
options: Sensory neurons at the base of the bud
Basal cells
Cells lining the taste pore
Supporting cells between olfactory neurons

q: A student places a few grains of salt on the very tip of her tongue. What does she taste?
options: A sweet taste
No taste until the salt reaches the sides of the tongue
A salty taste
A weak bitter taste

q: Daniel, 34, fell off his bike and struck the back of his head. Two weeks later he says food "has no taste". On testing, he correctly identifies sweet, salty, sour and bitter solutions placed on his tongue, but he cannot identify coffee or vanilla by sniffing. Which structures were most likely damaged?
options: The gustatory receptor cells in the taste buds of his tongue
Olfactory axons passing through the cribriform plate
The facial nerve on one side
The gustatory cortex in the insula

q: Put these steps in order, from an odorant entering the nose to the signal leaving the olfactory bulb.
options: The odorant dissolves in the mucus over the olfactory epithelium
It binds an odorant receptor protein on a cilium of an olfactory sensory neuron
A G protein switches on an enzyme that makes cAMP
cAMP opens cation channels, and chloride leaving the cell adds to the depolarization
Action potentials travel along the axon through the cribriform plate
The axon synapses in the olfactory bulb, and the olfactory tract carries the signal backward

q: Fill the gap: Salt dissolves in saliva → Na+ flows into a gustatory receptor cell through sodium channels → ______ → the cell releases more neurotransmitter → the sensory neuron fires action potentials faster
options: The gustatory receptor cell fires action potentials to the medulla
Na+ binds a G protein–coupled receptor protein
The gustatory receptor cell depolarizes
Basal cells divide to make more taste cells

q: This pathway traces a taste signal from the front of the tongue to the cortex. Which step is wrong?
options: A gustatory receptor cell releases neurotransmitter onto a sensory neuron
The signal travels in the facial nerve
The signal reaches a nucleus in the medulla oblongata
The signal relays in the olfactory bulb
The signal reaches the gustatory cortex in the insula

q: How does the olfactory pathway differ from the pathways of every other sense?
options: It reaches the cortex without first relaying in the thalamus
Its signals cross to the opposite side low in the spinal cord before rising
It uses no cranial nerve
Its sensory receptors have no axons

q: Which taste qualities are detected through G protein–coupled receptor proteins and a second messenger? Select all that apply.
options: Salty
Sweet
Sour
Umami
Bitter

q: A chemical blocks the enzyme that makes cAMP in olfactory sensory neurons. The person then sniffs a strong odorant. Predict the change in each variable, compared with the same sniff before the chemical.

variables.name: Odorant binding to odorant receptor proteins
Opening of cation channels in the cilia
Size of the neuron's receptor potential

q: A woman with a heavy cold and a blocked nose says her favorite curry "tastes like cardboard." What is the best explanation?
options: The cold virus has destroyed the gustatory receptor cells in her taste buds
Mucus has blocked her taste pores
Her facial nerve is inflamed
Odorants from the food cannot reach her olfactory epithelium

q: After throat surgery, a patient has reduced taste on the back third of his tongue only. Which nerve was most likely injured?
options: Facial nerve
Trigeminal nerve
Hypoglossal nerve
Glossopharyngeal nerve

q: Which chemical triggers the umami taste?
options: Hydrogen ions
Sodium ions
Glucose
Glutamate

q: The smell of a particular sunscreen instantly brings back a childhood beach holiday, along with the feelings that went with it. Which feature of the olfactory pathway best explains this?
options: Olfactory sensory neurons are replaced throughout life
Olfactory signals reach the amygdala and cortex near the hippocampus within two synapses
Olfactory signals are filtered by the thalamus before they reach the olfactory cortex
Odorant receptor proteins keep a record of odors met before

q: How does lemon juice produce a sour taste?
options: Hydrogen ions bind a G protein–coupled receptor protein on the microvilli of the cell
Hydrogen ions enter the cell through a proton channel and depolarize it
Hydrogen ions open chloride channels, and Cl− leaves the cell
Hydrogen ions stimulate trigeminal nociceptors

q: Humans have only about 400 kinds of odorant receptor protein, yet can tell apart far more odors than that. How?
options: Each olfactory sensory neuron makes all 400 kinds, so every neuron responds to every odor
Each odor has its own dedicated receptor protein, and new kinds are made as new odors are met
Each odorant binds several kinds of receptor protein, and the brain reads the pattern
The olfactory bulb makes up for the small number by adding extra kinds of synapse

q: After a viral illness, a man loses his sense of smell. Over the next four months it gradually returns. Which cells make this recovery possible?
options: Basal stem cells of the olfactory epithelium
Basal cells of the taste buds
Neurons of the olfactory cortex
Supporting cells, which turn into sensory neurons in adults

q: In most neurons, opening chloride channels makes the inside more negative. In an olfactory sensory neuron, opening chloride channels depolarizes the cell. Why?
options: Chloride in olfactory neurons carries a positive charge
These neurons hold so much chloride inside that Cl− flows out
Chloride channels in olfactory neurons let Na+ through as well
cAMP reverses the direction of every ion gradient in the cilia

q: The burning feeling from chili peppers is carried mainly by which sensory receptors?
options: Gustatory receptor cells that sense sour acids in the taste buds
Olfactory sensory neurons
Gustatory receptor cells for bitter
Heat-sensitive nociceptor endings of the trigeminal nerve

q: You drink a sweeter and a less sweet soda. Gustatory receptor cells have no axons. How does the stronger sweetness reach your brain as a stronger signal?
options: Taste cells release more neurotransmitter, so the sensory neurons fire faster
Each action potential in the taste nerve becomes larger and lasts longer
Sugar molecules travel along the facial nerve to the medulla
The taste cells send their own axons to the brain, but only when a stimulus is strong

q: Name the pinned structure.
options: Fovea centralis
Ciliary body
Optic disc
Choroid

fig.alt: A side view of the eyeball cut open. The wall has three layers: a tough white outer coat that becomes the clear dome at the front, a dark middle layer rich in blood vessels, and a thin yellow inner layer at the back with a small pit near its center and a pale spot where the optic nerve leaves. Behind the colored ring and its central opening sits the lens, held by fine threads to a ring of muscle and folded tissue. A small chamber lies in front of the lens and a large gel-filled chamber behind it. Muscles are attached above and below the eyeball.

q: Name the pinned structure.
options: Ciliary muscle
Iris
Zonule fibers
Scleral venous sinus

fig.alt: A side view of the eyeball cut open. The wall has three layers: a tough white outer coat that becomes the clear dome at the front, a dark middle layer rich in blood vessels, and a thin yellow inner layer at the back with a small pit near its center and a pale spot where the optic nerve leaves. Behind the colored ring and its central opening sits the lens, held by fine threads to a ring of muscle and folded tissue. A small chamber lies in front of the lens and a large gel-filled chamber behind it. Muscles are attached above and below the eyeball.

q: Name the pinned structure.
options: Optic tract
Lateral geniculate nucleus
Optic nerve
Optic chiasm

fig.alt: A view of the brain from below with both eyes at the front. Colored wedges show what each eye sees: the left half of the scene in purple and the right half in green, overlapping in the middle. Fibers from each eye run back in two nerves that meet in an X-shaped crossing just behind a small circle marking the pituitary gland; a few fibers leave the crossing for a small nucleus of the hypothalamus; fibers from the half of each retina nearer the nose cross to the other side, while those from the outer half stay on the same side. Behind the crossing, the green fibers all run on the left and the purple fibers on the right, to a relay in the thalamus on each side and then fan out to the visual cortex at the back of the brain.

q: Name the pinned structure.
options: Cornea
Conjunctiva
Sclera
Orbicularis oculi

fig.alt: A side view of the eye in its bony socket, cut through the middle. Fat fills the socket around the eyeball, and straight muscles run from the back of the socket to the eyeball, with the optic nerve between them. Above the eye, a long muscle runs forward into the upper eyelid. A thin ring of muscle lies in both eyelids under the skin, a thin membrane lines the inside of the lids and folds back over the white of the eye, and the clear dome at the front bulges out between the lids. The eyebrow and eyelashes are also shown.

q: Put the steps of tear flow in order, from where tears are made to where they drain.
options: The lacrimal gland releases tears through the lacrimal ducts
Blinking sweeps tears across the eye toward the inner corner
Tears enter the lacrimal puncta on the edges of the lids
The lacrimal canaliculi carry tears to the lacrimal sac
The nasolacrimal duct carries tears into the nose

q: After a blow to the head, Mr. Ruiz, 44, sees double when he walks down stairs or reads a book in his lap. When he looks toward his nose, his right eye cannot turn downward. Which muscle is weak?
options: Right inferior rectus
Right lateral rectus
Right superior oblique
Right superior rectus

q: Between age 30 and age 55, a woman's lenses gradually lose their flexibility. Predict the change in each variable when she tries to read a menu held close.

variables.name: How much the lens rounds up when the ciliary muscle contracts
Bending of light from the menu
Distance to the nearest point she can see sharply

misconception: presbyopia is the same as nearsightedness

q: You look up from a distant road sign to read a text message. What happens in your eye?
options: The ciliary muscle relaxes, the zonule fibers tighten and the lens flattens
The ciliary muscle contracts, the zonule fibers tighten and pull the lens rounder
The cornea bulges forward and bends light more strongly
The ciliary muscle contracts, the zonule fibers go slack and the lens rounds up
misconception: the ciliary muscle squeezes the lens round

q: A student wrote this sequence for focusing on a near object. Which step is wrong?
options: The oculomotor nerve carries parasympathetic signals to the eye
The ciliary muscle contracts and its ring becomes smaller
The zonule fibers are pulled tighter
The lens bulges into a rounder shape
Light from the near object is bent more and focuses on the retina

q: Standing 20 feet from a Snellen chart, a patient can read nothing smaller than the row labeled 60. What does her result mean?
options: She reads at 20 feet what a normal eye reads at 60 feet
She reads at 60 feet what a normal eye reads at 20 feet
Her vision is three times sharper than normal
She sees 60% of what a normal eye sees

q: An eyeball is slightly too long from front to back. Where does light from a distant object focus, and what lens corrects it?
options: Behind the retina; a convex lens
In front of the retina; a convex (converging) lens
Behind the retina; a concave lens
In front of the retina; a concave lens

q: A 10-year-old reads chapter books easily but squints to read the board from the back of the classroom. Her teacher notices she does better at the front. Which condition best fits?
options: Presbyopia
Hyperopia
Cataract
Myopia

q: Mrs. Adeyemi, 66, has had no eye pain, but her optometrist finds raised pressure in both eyes and loss of vision at the edges of both visual fields. The drainage of aqueous humor is slow. Which cells are being lost to cause her vision loss?
options: Rods in the periphery of the retina that see the edges of the field
Retinal ganglion cells, whose axons pass through the optic disc
Cells of the lens
Cells of the ciliary processes that secrete the aqueous humor

q: Which structures belong to the vascular tunic of the eye? Select all that apply.
options: Choroid
Sclera
Ciliary body
Retina
Iris
Cornea

q: Why is vision sharpest at the fovea?
options: Rods there feed many ganglion cells each, which multiplies their signal
It lies closest to the lens, so the image there is least blurred
Each cone has its own ganglion cell, and the layers above are pushed aside
It has the most blood vessels, so its photoreceptors receive the best oxygen supply

q: At night, a faint star seems to disappear when you look straight at it but reappears when you look slightly to one side. Why?
options: Its image moves off the cone-only fovea onto rods, which work in dim light
Looking straight at it bleaches the cones in the fovea
The optic disc lies at the center of the retina, directly behind the pupil and lens
Rods in the fovea adapt too quickly to a steady light

q: Put the steps of phototransduction in a rod in order, from a photon arriving to the signal reaching the bipolar cell.
options: Retinal changes from 11-cis to all-trans
Rhodopsin switches on the G protein transducin
An enzyme breaks down cGMP
cGMP-gated cation channels close
The rod hyperpolarizes
The rod releases less glutamate onto the bipolar cell

q: A rod has been in darkness. A flash of light now falls on it. Predict the change in each variable in the rod, compared with darkness.

variables.name: Membrane potential (how positive the inside is)

q: Complete the sequence for a rod in the dark: cGMP is high → cation channels stay open → ______ → the rod releases glutamate steadily.
options: The rod fires a steady stream of action potentials along its axon to the brain
Rhodopsin switches on transducin
Na+ flows in and keeps the rod depolarized at about −40 mV
K+ flows in and hyperpolarizes the rod

q: Using the absorbance curves, which cell type responds most strongly to light of 420 nm?
options: Rods
Short-wavelength ("blue") cones
Medium-wavelength ("green") cones
Long-wavelength ("red") cones

fig.alt: A graph of normalized absorbance, from 0 to 100, against wavelength of light from about 360 to 700 nanometers, with a color spectrum from violet to red under the axis. Four curves each rise to a peak and fall: a blue curve peaking at 420 nm, a dotted black curve peaking at 498 nm, a green curve peaking at 534 nm and a pink curve peaking at 564 nm. The curves overlap widely, especially the last two.

q: In very dim light only rods work. Using the curves, why can you see objects but not their colors?
options: Rods share one pigment, so they cannot tell wavelength from brightness
Rods absorb no light at wavelengths shorter than about 500 nm
Rods absorb every wavelength equally
Rods absorb best at a wavelength that almost no object in nature reflects

fig.alt: A graph of normalized absorbance, from 0 to 100, against wavelength of light from about 360 to 700 nanometers, with a color spectrum from violet to red under the axis. Four curves each rise to a peak and fall: a blue curve peaking at 420 nm, a dotted black curve peaking at 498 nm, a green curve peaking at 534 nm and a pink curve peaking at 564 nm. The curves overlap widely, especially the last two.

q: Mr. Chen, 52, keeps clipping doorframes and is startled by cars that seem to appear from nowhere on both sides. Testing shows he has lost the outer (temporal) half of the visual field of each eye. A scan shows a mass. Where is it most likely pressing?
options: The middle of the optic chiasm
The left optic tract
The right optic nerve
The occipital lobe on both sides

q: A stroke damages the right optic tract. What visual field loss results?
options: Blindness in the right eye
Loss of the outer half of both fields
Loss of the right half of the field in both eyes
Loss of the left half of the field in both eyes
misconception: each eye sends its signals only to the opposite hemisphere

q: Light shone into Ms. Park's left eye makes neither pupil narrow. Light shone into her right eye makes both pupils narrow. Where is the damage?
options: Left oculomotor nerve
Right oculomotor nerve
Left optic nerve
Right optic chiasm

q: A patient's pupils are very narrow, like pinpoints, in a normally lit room. What is this called, and which division of the autonomic nervous system narrows the pupil?
options: Mydriasis; sympathetic
Mydriasis; parasympathetic
Miosis; parasympathetic
Miosis; sympathetic

q: After a stroke, Mr. Olsen cannot say what a cup on the table is, or recognize his daughter's face, yet he reaches out and grasps the cup smoothly. Which part of visual processing is damaged?
options: The dorsal stream in the parietal lobe
The lateral geniculate nucleus
The optic chiasm
The ventral stream in the temporal lobe

q: Why is red–green color blindness far more common in males than in females?
options: Males have fewer cones in the fovea
Its pigment genes lie on the X chromosome, and males have only one X
Hormones made at puberty gradually damage the cone pigments in teenage boys
Males have more rods, which crowd out the cones

q: What happens at the moment a photon is absorbed by rhodopsin?
options: Retinal changes shape from its bent 11-cis form to the straight all-trans form
Opsin breaks down cGMP directly
The rod opens its cation channels
Retinal is carried away to the pigmented epithelium, where enzymes rebuild it

q: Put these in the order that light, and then the signal it starts, reaches them on the way from a scene to the cortex.
options: Cornea
Lens
Photoreceptors of the retina
Optic chiasm
Lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus
Primary visual cortex

q: Name the pinned structure.
options: Malleus
Stapes
Incus
Tympanic membrane

fig.alt: A cut through the side of the head showing the ear. On the outside, the flap of the ear leads into a canal through the skull bone that ends at a thin membrane. Behind the membrane is a small air-filled space colored red, holding a chain of three tiny bones; the last one sits in an opening in the bony wall of the inner ear. A tube runs down and forward from this space toward the throat. Deeper in the bone lie a snail-shaped coil, three looped canals above it and the chamber between them, with two nerve branches leaving toward the brain. Brackets under the drawing divide it into outer, middle and inner parts.

q: Name the pinned structure.
options: Ear canal
Auditory tube
Cochlear nerve
Semicircular canal

fig.alt: A cut through the side of the head showing the ear. On the outside, the flap of the ear leads into a canal through the skull bone that ends at a thin membrane. Behind the membrane is a small air-filled space colored red, holding a chain of three tiny bones; the last one sits in an opening in the bony wall of the inner ear. A tube runs down and forward from this space toward the throat. Deeper in the bone lie a snail-shaped coil, three looped canals above it and the chamber between them, with two nerve branches leaving toward the brain. Brackets under the drawing divide it into outer, middle and inner parts.

q: Name the pinned structure.
options: Tectorial membrane
Tympanic membrane
Scala tympani
Basilar membrane

fig.alt: A small drawing of the snail-shaped coil with a box around one turn, and an enlarged cross section of that turn. Inside the bony wall are three fluid-filled channels: an upper one, a small triangular middle one, and a lower one. On the floor of the middle channel sits a row of sensory cells covered by a flap of membrane. Nerve fibers run from these cells to a cluster of nerve cell bodies in the bony core and join a nerve bundle leaving the coil.

q: Name the pinned structure.
options: Cupula
Otolithic membrane
Macula
Tectorial membrane

fig.alt: Top left, the inner ear with the swelling at the base of one looped canal boxed. Below it, an enlarged cut through that swelling: a ridge of sensory cells whose projections stick up into a tall gel cap that spans the canal, with nerve fibers leaving from the base. Top right, a head turning. Bottom right, the same swelling while the head turns: the fluid in the canal lags behind, and red arrows show it bending the gel cap the opposite way to the turn.

q: Put the steps in order, from a sound entering the ear to the hair cells being stimulated.
options: Sound waves vibrate the tympanic membrane
The malleus, incus and stapes carry the vibration across the middle ear
The stapes rocks in the oval window
Pressure waves travel through the perilymph of the scala vestibuli
The basilar membrane vibrates
The hair cells' stereocilia bend

q: Put the stations of the auditory pathway in order, from the cochlea to the cortex.
options: Cochlear branch of the vestibulocochlear nerve
Cochlear nuclei
Superior olivary nuclei
Inferior colliculus
Medial geniculate nucleus of the thalamus
Primary auditory cortex in the temporal lobe

q: After a cold, fluid fills a child's left middle ear. Predict the change in each variable on the left side, compared with before the cold.

variables.name: Movement of the tympanic membrane in response to sound
Vibration passed along the ossicles to the oval window
Quietest sound heard through the air (hearing threshold)
Response of the cochlea to a tuning fork pressed on the skull
Loudness in the left ear of a tuning fork placed on the forehead

q: A smoke alarm gives a high-pitched 4,000 Hz tone. Where on the basilar membrane is the vibration largest?
options: Near the apex, where the membrane is wide and floppy
Evenly along the whole length of the membrane
Near the base, where the membrane is narrow and stiff
At the round window, where the membrane ends
misconception: pitch is coded by how fast the whole basilar membrane vibrates

q: Mr. Brandt, 61, has operated a jackhammer for 30 years. His hearing test shows loss mainly at high frequencies, around 4,000 Hz, in both ears. Both Rinne tests show air conduction better than bone. Where is the damage most likely?
options: Outer hair cells near the base of each cochlea
The ossicles of both middle ears
Inner and outer hair cells near the apex of each cochlea
Both primary auditory cortices

q: The stereocilia of a hair cell are pushed toward the tallest stereocilium. What happens to the hair cell?
options: Tip links slacken, channels close and the cell hyperpolarizes
Tip links stretch, channels open, K+ flows in and the cell depolarizes
The hair cell fires an action potential along its axon to the brainstem
Tip links stretch, channels open, K+ flows out and the cell hyperpolarizes

q: In most neurons, opening K+ channels lets K+ leave and hyperpolarizes the cell. Why does opening the channels in a cochlear hair cell's stereocilia let K+ in and depolarize it?
options: Their tips sit in endolymph, which is rich in K+ and positively charged
Hair cells keep almost no K+ inside, so any open K+ channel lets K+ rush in
The channels pump K+ in using ATP
K+ carries a negative charge in endolymph

q: Fill the gap: stereocilia bend toward the tallest → tip links stretch → ______ → the hair cell depolarizes → voltage-gated Ca2+ channels open → the hair cell releases more glutamate.
options: Mechanically gated channels open and K+ flows in from the endolymph
Voltage-gated Na+ channels open and the hair cell fires an action potential
The tectorial membrane releases neurotransmitter
Otoliths slide across the hair cells

q: A student traced how a sound reaches the brain from a cochlear hair cell. Which step is wrong?
options: The basilar membrane moves under the tectorial membrane and the stereocilia bend
Mechanically gated channels open and the hair cell depolarizes
The hair cell fires action potentials along its own axon in the cochlear nerve
Sensory neurons of the spiral ganglion fire faster
Signals reach the cochlear nuclei in the brainstem

q: Ms. Abara, 34, has muffled hearing in her right ear. In the Weber test she hears the tuning fork louder in her right ear. In the Rinne test on the right, she hears the fork longer on the mastoid process than beside the ear canal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Sensorineural hearing loss in the right ear
Conductive hearing loss in the right ear
Sensorineural hearing loss in the left ear
Conductive hearing loss in the left ear

q: A patient hears the Weber tuning fork louder in his right ear. His Rinne test shows air conduction better than bone conduction in both ears. Which is the most likely finding?
options: Conductive hearing loss in the right ear
Conductive hearing loss in the left ear
Normal hearing in both ears
Sensorineural hearing loss in the left ear

q: In otosclerosis, abnormal bone growth fixes the stapes so it cannot move in the oval window. What kind of hearing loss results, and what will the Rinne test show on that side?
options: Sensorineural; air conduction better than bone
Conductive; air conduction better than bone
Conductive; bone conduction better than air
Sensorineural; bone conduction better than air

q: You turn up the volume on a song without changing its notes. How does your cochlea signal the louder sound?
options: The traveling wave now peaks at a different place along the basilar membrane
The membrane moves farther and more sensory neurons fire, and fire faster
Only the outer hair cells respond to loud sounds
Each action potential in the cochlear nerve becomes larger

q: As a plane descends, your hearing becomes muffled until you swallow and your ears "pop." What did the swallow do?
options: It closed the auditory tube so outside air could no longer reach the eardrum
It moved the stapes back into the oval window
It drained fluid from the cochlea into the throat
It opened the auditory tube, equalizing pressure across the eardrum

q: A stroke destroys the primary auditory cortex on the left side only. What happens to the patient's hearing?
options: He is deaf in the right ear
He is deaf in the left ear
Neither ear goes deaf, since each ear reaches both hemispheres
He loses the ability to hear high-pitched sounds in both of his ears
misconception: each ear sends signals only to the opposite hemisphere

q: A lift starts to rise. Which part of the vestibular apparatus is best placed to sense this?
options: The saccule, whose macula lies roughly vertical
The utricle, whose macula lies roughly horizontal
The lateral semicircular canal
The cochlear duct

q: A child spins in a chair for a minute and then stops suddenly. She feels as if she is spinning the other way. Why?
options: Otoliths have come loose from the maculae
The endolymph keeps flowing and bends the cupula the opposite way
The cupula is heavy and is pulled downhill by gravity when she stops
The vestibulocochlear nerve keeps firing from fatigue

q: Which structures belong to the vestibular apparatus? Select all that apply.
options: Utricle
Basilar membrane
Saccule
Semicircular canals
Tympanic membrane
Scala vestibuli

q: You turn your head quickly to the right while reading a sign. Through the vestibulo-ocular reflex, what do your eyes do?
options: Both eyes turn right, ahead of the head
Only the right eye turns left
Both eyes stay fixed in their sockets and the image slides
Both eyes turn left by the same amount

q: The tympanic membrane has about 17 times the area of the stapes footplate. What does this do to sound reaching the inner ear?
options: It raises the pressure at the oval window, so less sound is reflected
It lowers the frequency of the sound so that the cochlea can detect it
It protects the cochlea by reducing the pressure of loud sounds
It lets sound bypass the ossicles

q: What does the round window do during hearing?
options: It lets the stapes push air from the middle ear into the inner ear
It bulges outward each time the stapes pushes inward
It connects the cochlea to the semicircular canals
It drains endolymph into the middle ear
